lesson.title: Paying for Reach: The Business of Transit
lesson.summary: A transit provider is a network that sells a customer full reachability to the rest of the internet, advertising the customer's routes everywhere and the provider's entire routing table back to the customer, in exchange for payment.
lesson.body:
Not every relationship between two autonomous systems is a peering relationship, and most networks, including nearly every network that is not tier 1, need some way to reach destinations far outside anything their direct peers can offer. That is the role a transit provider fills: it is a network that sells a customer access to the rest of the internet, not just to its own customers, in exchange for payment. Buying transit is the most straightforward way for any network, from a small regional ISP up to a very large national one, to guarantee it can reach every destination on the internet without having to negotiate a peering agreement with every network that might ever originate traffic destined for it.

The mechanics of a transit relationship look almost like a mirror image of peering's narrower rule. When a network buys transit, its provider advertises the customer's routes onward to essentially everyone else the provider is connected to, including its own peers and its own upstream providers if it has any, because fully advertising a paying customer's reachability outward is exactly the service being sold. Going the other direction, the provider also advertises to the customer, not just its own routes and its own customers' routes the way a peer would, but its entire view of the internet: everything the provider itself can reach, whether through its own peering, its own transit purchases, or its own customers. That asymmetry, the provider does the work of reaching the whole internet on the customer's behalf and gets paid for it, while a peer only ever offers its own customers for free, is the entire economic and technical distinction between the two kinds of interdomain relationship.

A single autonomous system very often holds both kinds of relationship at once toward different neighbors: it might buy transit from one or two upstream providers to guarantee full reachability as a safety net, while also peering directly, settlement free, with other networks it exchanges enough traffic with to make a direct connection worthwhile, reserving paid transit for everything else. Tier 1 networks are simply the limiting case at the top of this picture, the networks that have negotiated enough settlement free peering that they never need to buy transit from anyone at all, which is exactly the definition given earlier, and the reason transit and peering, together, are what actually stitch the loosely hierarchical internet topology described earlier into a single connected whole.
